contents.text: All of the substances around you are composed of chemical elements. Scientists represent these substances using chemical formulas and models.

pieces.text: The
for a substance tells you which chemical elements the substance is composed of. In a chemical formula, each chemical element is represented by its
. A chemical symbol may consist of one capital letter or one capital letter followed by a lowercase letter.

subpoints.text: In a model, the atoms in a substance are often represented as balls, and bonds can be represented as sticks. The balls in most models are not all the same color. for a substance contains the chemical symbol for each element in the substance. Many chemical formulas also contain subscripts. A
is small text placed lower than the normal line of text. Each subscript in a chemical formula is placed
the symbol for an element and tells you how many atoms of that element that symbol represents. If there is no subscript after a symbol, that symbol represents one atom.

So, the chemical formula for a substance tells you which elements make up that substance. It also tells you the ratio of the atoms of those elements in the substance. For example, the chemical formula below tells you that there are

content.text: three chlorine atoms for every one boron atom

pieces.text: in the substance. This chemical formula represents the same substance as the ball-and-stick model shown above.

subheader.text: How can atoms bond together in a molecule?

pieces.text: One way atoms can bond together is by sharing
. You can think of electrons as tiny particles in the outermost part of an atom. When two atoms share electrons, the atoms bond together.

contents.text: In a ball-and-stick model of a molecule, each stick represents two shared electrons. So, a model with two balls connected by one stick represents two atoms that share two electrons. A model with two balls connected by two sticks represents two atoms that share four electrons.

subheader.text: How can atoms bond together in a molecule?

pieces.text: One way atoms can bond together is by sharing
. You can think of electrons as tiny particles in the outermost part of an atom. When two atoms share electrons, the atoms bond together.

contents.text: In a ball-and-stick model of a molecule, each stick represents two shared electrons. So, a model with two balls connected by one stick represents two atoms that share two electrons. A model with two balls connected by two sticks represents two atoms that share four electrons.

subheader.text: How can atoms bond together in a molecule?

pieces.text: One way atoms can bond together is by sharing
. You can think of electrons as tiny particles in the outermost part of an atom. When two atoms share electrons, the atoms bond together.

contents.text: In a ball-and-stick model of a molecule, each stick represents two shared electrons. So, a model with two balls connected by one stick represents two atoms that share two electrons. A model with two balls connected by two sticks represents two atoms that share four electrons.
Ball-and-stick models of three molecules are shown below:

alternativeText.text: A model of a molecule containing two balls labeled F.

mainText.text: The atoms in a fluorine molecule share two electrons.

mainText.text: The atoms in an oxygen molecule share four electrons.

subheader.text: How can atoms bond together in a molecule?

pieces.text: One way atoms can bond together is by sharing
. You can think of electrons as tiny particles in the outermost part of an atom. When two atoms share electrons, the atoms bond together.

contents.text: In a ball-and-stick model of a molecule, each stick represents two shared electrons. So, a model with two balls connected by one stick represents two atoms that share two electrons. A model with two balls connected by two sticks represents two atoms that share four electrons.
Ball-and-stick models of three molecules are shown below:

mainText.text: The atoms in a fluorine molecule share two electrons.

alternativeText.text: A model of a molecule containing two balls labeled O.

mainText.text: The atoms in an oxygen molecule share four electrons.
